headline: A robot runs 100 meters faster than any human

sources.title: Chinese humanoid robots smash records in 100m sprint and high jump at Beijing robot games (AP via ABC News)
China's humanoid robots put machines to the test in global competition (NBC)
Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record at humanoid games (Al Jazeera)
Historic first as Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record at Beijing games (video, BBC News)

chunks.text: The runners {{lined up}} in Beijing, but these [[athletes]] were made of metal. At the second World Humanoid Robot Games in late August, a Chinese robot ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds. That is faster than the human [[world record]] of 9.58 seconds, set by Usain Bolt in 2009. The machine {{sped up}} [[smoothly]] down the [[track]], crossed the [[finish line]], and then {{ended up}} in a [[padded wall]] because it could not stop in time. Fans {{cheered on}} the machines anyway.

verbs.correct: To stand in a row before a start
verbs.wrong: To practice before a big race
verbs.why: Sprinters line up in their lanes, and kids line up before class. In Beijing, robot runners lined up just like human athletes.
Trains speed up after leaving the station, and songs speed up near the end. The robot sped up smoothly and beat the fastest human time in history.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a place
verbs.wrong: To win by a small distance
verbs.why: A lost tourist can end up at the wrong hotel, and a bad throw can end up in the crowd. The winning robot ended up in a padded wall because it could not stop.
Parents cheer on their kids at games, and whole cities cheer on their teams. The fans in Beijing cheered on the machines like real athletes.

chunks.text: More than 2,000 [[humanoid robots]] from 16 countries, including Germany, Japan, and the United States, {{took on}} the world's best records and each other in 51 events, from soccer and table tennis to [[weightlifting]] and [[tug of war]]. Another machine jumped 2.88 meters in the standing [[high jump]], higher than any human has ever jumped. There were plenty of [[failures]], too. Robots {{fell over}}, crashed, and sent [[sparks]] flying. Some {{got up}} by themselves and kept going, and that [[impressed]] the crowd most of all.

verbs.why: A small team can take on the champions, and a new phone can take on the market leader. These robots took on the best human records ever set.

verbs.correct: To drop to the ground from standing
verbs.why: Toddlers fall over when they learn to walk, and bikes fall over in strong wind. Plenty of robots fell over on the track in Beijing.
Boxers get up before the count of ten, and skaters get up after every fall. Some robots got up by themselves, and the crowd loved it.

chunks.text: Between events, teams {{plugged in}} their machines to charge batteries and replace [[spare parts]]. For China, the games are about much more than sport. The country's robot [[industry]] has {{taken off}}, with [[government support]] and hundreds of companies building machines for factories, hospitals, and homes. China now produces about 82 percent of the world's humanoid robots, and other countries are racing to {{catch up}}. The United States recently [[restricted]] [[imports]] of foreign humanoid robots, calling them a [[national security]] question.

verbs.why: You plug in a phone at night and plug in a lamp by the couch. Between events, teams plugged in their robots to charge the batteries.
A small app can take off overnight, and sales take off before the holidays. China's robot industry has taken off with strong government support.

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as others
verbs.why: Students catch up after missing class, and slow starters catch up by the finish. Other countries are now racing to catch up with China's robot industry.

chunks.text: So how close are robot workers, really? Experts say the technology has {{come along}} fast, but most humanoid robots are still used for shows, [[research]], and [[demonstrations]], not for daily jobs. A machine that runs like a [[champion]] can still fail to [[pour]] a cup of coffee. The games {{showed off}} both sides of that story: amazing speed, and a long distance still to go.

verbs.why: A student's English comes along with practice, and a garden comes along by summer. Experts say robot technology has come along amazingly fast.

verbs.wrong: To sell something at a fair
verbs.why: Kids show off new sneakers, and companies show off their latest products. The games showed off both the speed and the limits of today's robots.

mainIdea.s: At robot games in Beijing, machines beat famous human records in running and jumping, though many also crashed or fell. The event showed how fast China's robot industry is growing.
mainIdea.why: A robot beat the fastest 100 meter time in history, but experts say most robots are still far from doing daily jobs.

mainIdea.s: Machines competed in dozens of sports at a big event in China but could not get close to any human records. Experts said the technology is improving far more slowly than they expected.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the robots did beat human records, in both the 100 meter sprint and the standing high jump.

mainIdea.s: Factory robots from sixteen countries competed in Beijing to see which could build cars and sort packages fastest. The winning machines will start work in hospitals early next year.
mainIdea.why: The games featured sports like sprinting and soccer, not factory work, and no jobs were promised to the winners.

tf.s: A robot ran 100 meters faster than Usain Bolt's world record
tf.why: The winning robot finished in 9.39 seconds, quicker than Bolt's 9.58 from 2009.

tf.s: The winning robot stopped perfectly at the finish line
tf.why: It ended up in a padded wall because it could not stop in time.

tf.s: Robots took on each other in 51 different events
tf.why: The events ranged from soccer and table tennis to weightlifting and tug of war.

tf.s: Every robot that fell over had to be carried off the track
tf.why: Some got up by themselves and kept going, which impressed the crowd most of all.

tf.s: Experts say humanoid robots are ready to replace human workers now
tf.why: Most are still used for shows, research, and demonstrations, not for daily jobs.

tf.s: China produces most of the world's humanoid robots
tf.why: About 82 percent, and its robot industry has taken off with government support.
